items.setupText: Choose the pronoun that refers to the book, not Mina.
items.taskText: Mina has a book. ___ is on the desk.
options: They
It
Them
She
items.answer: It
items.explanation: It refers to the one book and agrees with is.

rationales.It: It refers to the one book and agrees with is.
rationales.They: They would refer to more than one book and would need are.
rationales.Them: Them is an object form; this sentence needs a subject before is.
rationales.She: She would refer to Mina, not the book specified in the task.

findings: The original did not explicitly identify the intended reference and dismissed all distractors with generic feedback.

items.setupText: Choose the form for the person speaking, using standard English.
items.taskText: Hello. ___ am your new neighbour.
options: Me
My
Mine
I
items.answer: I
items.explanation: I is the subject form for the speaker and pairs with am.

rationales.Me: Me is used as an object; a subject is needed before am.
rationales.I: I is the subject form for the speaker and pairs with am.
rationales.My: My introduces a noun, as in my name; it cannot stand as the subject here.
rationales.Mine: Mine refers to something belonging to the speaker, not the speaker introducing themself.

findings: The girl-in-class item repeated in class and gave no explanation of subject form.
audit.microSkill: First-person subject in an introduction
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates the speaker pronoun from object and ownership forms.
audit.levelReason: A neighbour's introduction uses familiar A1 language and am.
audit.similarityNote: Direct self-introduction instead of third-person school description.

items.setupText: Choose the subject pronoun referring to the photos.
items.taskText: Here are the holiday photos. ___ are ready to print.
options: They
Them
Their
It
items.answer: They
items.explanation: They is the plural subject pronoun referring to the photos.

rationales.Their: Their shows possession before a noun; it does not replace the photos by itself.
rationales.They: They is the plural subject pronoun referring to the photos.
rationales.It: It would refer to one photo and require is, not are.

findings: The boys-playing-soccer frame was repeated four times with only time or place changes.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that they refers to plural objects as well as people.
audit.levelReason: A short photo-printing exchange provides a visible plural reference.

me
my
mine

rationales.my: 'My' needs a following noun, such as 'my phone'.

items.setupText: Choose the form meaning that the keys belong to the person being addressed.
items.taskText: Are these ___ keys, Mr Shah?

you
yours
yourself
items.answer: your

rationales.you: You names the listener but cannot introduce the noun keys as a possessive.
rationales.yours: Yours stands alone; before keys, use your.

items.taskText: The blue bag belongs to me. It is ___.

mine
me
I

rationales.mine: 'Mine' replaces 'my bag' and can stand after 'is'.
rationales.me: 'Me' refers to the speaker, not to something the speaker owns.
rationales.I: 'I' is a subject pronoun and does not express bag ownership here.

items.setupText: Choose the subject pronoun for the speaker and her husband together.
items.taskText: My husband and I live near the station. ___ walk to work.

They
Our
We
items.answer: We
items.explanation: We includes the speaker and the other person, her husband.

rationales.They: They would exclude the speaker from the group described.
rationales.We: We includes the speaker and the other person, her husband.
rationales.Our: Our needs a following noun, such as our office, and cannot replace the two people alone.

items.setupText: Choose the object pronoun for the speaker and her friend.

options: us
we
our
ours
items.answer: us
items.explanation: Us is the object pronoun for the speaker and her friend together.

rationales.our: Our would need a noun naming something belonging to the group.
rationales.ours: Ours expresses ownership, not the people needing help.

items.taskText: This coat belongs to my sister. It is ___.

she
hers
herself

rationales.her: 'Her' shows possession before a noun, but the noun 'coat' is omitted here.
rationales.she: 'She' refers to the sister as a person, not her coat.
rationales.herself: 'Herself' refers back to the sister, not to a possession.

items.setupText: Choose the word showing that the tickets belong to both neighbours.
items.taskText: Our neighbours are going to a concert. These are ___ tickets.
options: them
theirs
they
their
items.answer: their
items.explanation: Their introduces tickets and links ownership to the neighbours.

rationales.them: Them is an object pronoun, not the form used before an owned noun.
rationales.their: Their introduces tickets and links ownership to the neighbours.
rationales.theirs: Theirs would stand alone after are; before tickets, use their.
rationales.they: They is a subject pronoun and cannot show ownership before tickets.

findings: The missing-pencil question changed only the kitchen location and retained generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Their for plural possessors before a noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects a plural owner group to its possessions.
audit.levelReason: Concert tickets and two neighbours provide straightforward plural reference.
audit.similarityNote: Plural possession, distinct from the individual listener's your keys.

items.setupText: Choose the pronoun that refers to the two parcels as the things to bring.
items.taskText: Two parcels are at reception. Please bring ___ upstairs.
options: they
their
it
them
items.answer: them
items.explanation: Them is the plural object pronoun referring to the two parcels.

rationales.they: They is a subject form, not the object of bring.
rationales.their: Their introduces a possessed noun; it does not replace parcels on its own.
rationales.them: Them is the plural object pronoun referring to the two parcels.
rationales.it: It would refer to one parcel rather than both of them.

findings: The Hana-and-book item was another name-only variation of the first question.
audit.microSkill: Them as a plural object for delivered things
audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts they as a subject with them as the object of a request.
audit.levelReason: A reception delivery is concrete and uses a short imperative.
audit.similarityNote: Object reference to parcels complements subject reference to photos without repeating the sentence frame.

items.setupText: Choose the form that refers to my father as the subject, in standard English.
items.taskText: My father is a bus driver. ___ starts work early.
options: Him
His
He
Himself
items.answer: He
items.explanation: He is the subject pronoun referring back to my father.

rationales.Him: Him is an object form, not a subject before starts.
rationales.His: His can show ownership, but it does not replace the father as the person starting work.
rationales.Himself: Himself normally refers back to a subject or adds emphasis; it is not the ordinary subject pronoun needed here.
rationales.He: He is the subject pronoun referring back to my father.

findings: The girl-with-red-bag item only added by the window and did not explain pronoun roles.
audit.microSkill: He as a personal subject rather than an object or possessive
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies the person carrying out an action using the subject form.
audit.levelReason: A family member's work schedule is familiar beginner content.
audit.similarityNote: Masculine personal subject contrasted with its related forms, not with unrelated plural people.

items.setupText: Choose the word for the woman receiving the invitation.
items.taskText: My aunt lives nearby. I invited ___ to dinner.
options: her
she
hers
herself
items.answer: her
items.explanation: Her is the object form for the aunt who receives the invitation.

rationales.her: Her is the object form for the aunt who receives the invitation.
rationales.she: She would be a subject; after invited, use the object form her.
rationales.hers: Hers means something belonging to the aunt, not the aunt herself.
rationales.herself: The subject is I, so herself does not express the speaker inviting the aunt in this sentence.

findings: The soccer-before-dinner variant added no distinct pronoun or feedback demand.
audit.microSkill: Her as an object referring to a woman
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes her as a person receiving an action from hers as a possession.

items.setupText: Choose the word that means 'his phone' without repeating 'phone'.
items.taskText: This phone belongs to my brother. The phone is ___.
options: he
him
himself
his
items.answer: his
items.explanation: 'His' can stand alone to mean 'his phone'; its form does not change when the noun is omitted.

rationales.he: 'He' refers to the brother as a person and does not express ownership here.
rationales.his: 'His' can stand alone to mean 'his phone'; its form does not change when the noun is omitted.
rationales.him: 'Him' is an object pronoun, not a possessive form.
rationales.himself: 'Himself' refers to the brother, not to an object belonging to him.

findings: The morning-teacher question reused the same us/we/our/ours choice without explanation.
audit.microSkill: His retaining its form when the noun is omitted
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that his differs from pairs such as her/hers and my/mine.
audit.levelReason: A familiar phone with an explicit owner supports the form contrast.
audit.similarityNote: An unchanged possessive form rather than another hers-style ending.

items.setupText: Choose the word for the person I am speaking to.
items.taskText: Hello, Ms Chen. Are ___ here for the interview?
options: your
you
yours
yourself
items.answer: you
items.explanation: You addresses Ms Chen directly and works as the subject after are.

rationales.your: Your must introduce a noun, such as your interview.
rationales.yours: Yours refers to something belonging to the listener, not the listener attending.
rationales.you: You addresses Ms Chen directly and works as the subject after are.
rationales.yourself: Yourself is not the ordinary personal subject in this question; use you.

findings: The boy's-pencil item was repeated again with only on the bus added.
audit.microSkill: You as the subject in direct address
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects second-person reference to a named listener in a question.
audit.levelReason: An interview reception question uses a short familiar pattern.
audit.similarityNote: Direct address in an inverted question, not possession of the listener's keys.

items.setupText: Choose the standard word used as the subject in this weather sentence.
items.taskText: Take an umbrella. ___ is raining.
options: This
There
It
They
items.answer: It
items.explanation: Weather expressions use it as a subject even though it does not stand for a particular object.

rationales.This: This would point to an identified thing; the ordinary weather sentence uses it without such a reference.
rationales.There: There is raining is not the standard weather construction; use it is raining.
rationales.They: They needs are and refers to people or things, not the weather subject here.
rationales.It: Weather expressions use it as a subject even though it does not stand for a particular object.

findings: The Luis-and-book item repeated the same reference frame for a fourth time.
audit.microSkill: Nonreferential it in a weather expression
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that some uses of it do not replace an earlier noun.
audit.levelReason: Rain and an umbrella give an immediately understandable weather context.
audit.similarityNote: Weather it contrasts with it referring to the book in 2641.

items.setupText: Choose the question asking for the new person's identity, not a place, time or choice of object.
items.taskText: Someone has just joined our table. ___ is that?
options: Where
When
Who
Which
items.answer: Who
items.explanation: Who asks which person has joined the table.

rationales.Who: Who asks which person has joined the table.
rationales.Where: Where asks about a place, not the person's identity.
rationales.When: When asks about time rather than who the person is.
rationales.Which: Which asks someone to select from an identified set; no such set is supplied here.

findings: The red-bag-with-the-teacher version retained the repeated classroom frame and vague task.
audit.microSkill: Who asking for a person's identity
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses an interrogative pronoun to request a missing person reference.
audit.levelReason: A person joining a table creates a simple social question.
audit.similarityNote: Requests an identity instead of referring back to an already named person.

items.setupText: Choose the pronoun for one item I am holding here, not an item farther away.
items.taskText: At the shop, I hold up a mug and ask, 'How much is ___?'
options: these
those
this
that
items.answer: this
items.explanation: This can stand alone for the single mug held near the speaker.

rationales.these: These refers to more than one nearby item and would need are.
rationales.this: This can stand alone for the single mug held near the speaker.
rationales.those: Those points to plural items farther away, not this one mug.
rationales.that: That normally points to an item farther away; the task explicitly asks for the nearby reference.

findings: The boys-before-the-bell question repeated the plural subject frame with another school tail.
audit.microSkill: This as a standalone nearby singular reference
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses a demonstrative pronoun without repeating the object name.
audit.levelReason: Holding up one mug makes proximity and number concrete.

items.setupText: Choose the pronoun for several items over there, not items near me.
items.taskText: The shoes are across the room. I point and say, 'I like ___.'
options: that
those
this
these
items.answer: those

rationales.this: This is singular and near the speaker, unlike the shoes across the room.
rationales.those: Those stands for the plural shoes at a distance.
rationales.these: These normally identifies nearby plural items; the task specifies items over there.

audit.microSkill: Those as a distant plural pronoun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Combines plural reference and distance without repeating a noun.
audit.levelReason: Pointing across a room makes the intended distance visible in the context.
audit.similarityNote: Distant plural object reference contrasts with the nearby singular mug.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase for an apartment belonging to the speaker and his partner, without repeating 'apartment'.
items.taskText: My partner and I own this apartment. It is ___.
options: ours
us
our
we

rationales.our: 'Our' needs a noun after it, such as 'our apartment'.
rationales.we: 'We' is the subject form for the owners and does not express possession after 'is'.
rationales.ours: 'Ours' stands alone for 'our apartment' and includes the speaker among the owners.

themselves
herself
another person

rationales.each other: Each other describes the two people sending messages to one another.

them
one
ones

It refers to a decision that the committee had already reached.
It introduces the later action that the committee found difficult.
It replaces the committee to avoid repeating that noun.
items.answer: It introduces the later action that the committee found difficult.
items.explanation: 'Find it difficult to do something' uses 'it' before an adjective and a later infinitive clause; no previously named object is required.

rationales.It refers to the deadline as a difficult: The difficulty concerns reaching a decision in time, not the deadline as an object.
rationales.It refers to a decision that the committ: The sentence does not establish a completed decision; the assessed action is to reach one.
rationales.It replaces the committee to avoid repea: The committee is the finder or evaluator; 'it' is not a second reference to that group here.
rationales.It introduces the later action that the: 'Find it difficult to do something' uses 'it' before an adjective and a later infinitive clause; no previously named object is required.

The guide has received confirmation of Friday's reopening.
The bridge will remain closed on Friday.
Friday will suit the visitor's plans better than another day.

'So' stands for the proposition in the question; the guide hopes that reopening on Friday will happen.

items.setupText: Replace 'did so' with an explicit action to say that Nadia fulfilled her promise after forwarding the files, not merely that she made the promise then.

She deleted the draft files after forwarding them to the archivist.
She forwarded the draft files after deleting them from the archive.
She kept the draft files after forwarding them to the archivist.
items.answer: She deleted the draft files after forwarding them to the archivist.
items.explanation: The explicit verb 'deleted' selects performance of the promised action. 'Them' still refers to the files that were forwarded beforehand.

rationales.She made the promise after forwarding th: This explicitly dates the promise, but the brief requires the later action that fulfilled it.
rationales.She deleted the draft files after forwar: The explicit verb 'deleted' selects performance of the promised action. 'Them' still refers to the files that were forwarded beforehand.
rationales.She forwarded the draft files after dele: This reverses the stated forwarding/deletion order and changes the deletion location.
rationales.She kept the draft files after forwardin: Keeping the files would not fulfill the stated promise to delete them.

items.setupText: Choose the intended audience reference of 'we' in this sentence from a report.
items.taskText: As we can see from Table 2, demand rose during the summer. The report does not identify its readers as members of the research team.
options: The writer states that every reader helped collect the data.
The writer excludes readers and refers only to the people shown in the table.
The writer invites readers to examine the table together.
The writer claims that the table was written jointly by all readers.
items.answer: The writer invites readers to examine the table together.
items.explanation: 'We' can include writer and readers in a shared act of looking at evidence without making them a single research team.

rationales.The writer states that every reader help: Inclusive 'we' in presenting a table does not establish participation in data collection.
rationales.The writer excludes readers and refers o: 'As we can see' addresses the act of examining the table, not necessarily its subjects.
rationales.The writer invites readers to examine th: 'We' can include writer and readers in a shared act of looking at evidence without making them a single research team.
rationales.The writer claims that the table was wri: Inviting readers to observe a table does not attribute its authorship to them.

audit.microSkill: Reader-inclusive we in explanatory prose
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes rhetorical inclusion in observation from actual participation in producing evidence.
audit.levelReason: The learner interprets a conventional report voice without turning an audience relationship into an authorship claim.
audit.similarityNote: Rhetorical writer-reader group, unlike literal first-person groups at A1.

items.setupText: Choose what 'those of us who' identifies without including the whole group.
items.taskText: Those of us who work weekends need access cards that function outside normal office hours.
options: All employees, whether or not they work weekends.
The weekend workers within a group that includes the speaker.
Only employees outside the speaker's group.
The speaker alone, excluding the other weekend workers.
items.answer: The weekend workers within a group that includes the speaker.
items.explanation: 'Of us' supplies the larger speaker-inclusive group; 'who work weekends' selects the relevant members. The wording does not by itself say that the speaker belongs to that subset.

rationales.All employees, whether or not they work: 'Who work weekends' restricts the larger 'us' group to its weekend-working members.
rationales.Only employees outside the speaker's gro: 'Of us' explicitly places the selected people within a speaker-inclusive group.
rationales.The speaker alone, excluding the other w: 'Those' is plural and does not select only the speaker.
rationales.The weekend workers within a group that: 'Of us' supplies the larger speaker-inclusive group; 'who work weekends' selects the relevant members. The wording does not by itself say that the speaker belongs to that subset.

findings: The evaluation-memo applicant sentence recycled the same whom choice with an appended context.
audit.microSkill: Subset reference within a speaker-inclusive group
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes membership in the larger us group from membership in the relative-clause subset.
audit.levelReason: The reader must track both the group supplied by us and the restriction supplied by who work weekends.
audit.similarityNote: Nested personal group reference, not simple those who applied to all residents.

items.setupText: Choose the accurate account of 'they' in this conditional instruction.
items.taskText: If a guest needs a quieter room, they should contact reception. The notice names no particular guest.
options: They refers to whichever individual guest meets the stated condition.
They proves that several guests have already complained.
They refers to the reception staff who receive the request.
They requires the notice to have named the guest in an earlier sentence.
items.answer: They refers to whichever individual guest meets the stated condition.
items.explanation: The conditional introduces a possible guest, and singular 'they' continues that reference without identifying an actual person in advance.

rationales.They refers to whichever individual gues: The conditional introduces a possible guest, and singular 'they' continues that reference without identifying an actual person in advance.
rationales.They proves that several guests have alr: The instruction is conditional; the pronoun establishes neither actual complaints nor a plural guest count.
rationales.They refers to the reception staff who r: The guest is the person instructed to contact reception, not the staff receiving contact.
rationales.They requires the notice to have named t: A conditional can introduce a hypothetical person whose reference continues into the instruction.

findings: The draft-report newer-one sentence repeated a basic substitution choice with no added B2 demand.
audit.microSkill: Personal reference introduced within a condition
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses a pronoun for a hypothetical individual without inferring an actual named or plural group.
audit.levelReason: The learner distinguishes reference continuity from a claim that the condition has already been met.
audit.similarityNote: Hypothetical guest reference, distinct from each applicant's general distributive instruction.

items.setupText: Choose the accurate assessment of the editor's attempted clarification.
items.taskText: Draft: 'The editor told the translator that they had missed the deadline.' Edit: 'The editor told the translator that he had missed the deadline.' No gender or deadline-holder is identified elsewhere.
options: The edit makes the translator the deadline-holder because he follows translator.
The edit assumes gender without settling which of the two people missed the deadline.
The edit establishes that only the editor could have missed the deadline.
The edit merely corrects a plural pronoun that could not refer to either individual.
items.answer: The edit assumes gender without settling which of the two people missed the deadline.
items.explanation: Singular they can refer to either person here. Replacing it with he supplies an unsupported gender choice but does not resolve the competing references.

rationales.The edit makes the translator the deadli: The nearest noun is not a binding rule for personal reference; he could still be read as referring to the editor.
rationales.The edit assumes gender without settling: Singular they can refer to either person here. Replacing it with he supplies an unsupported gender choice but does not resolve the competing references.
rationales.The edit establishes that only the edito: Subject status in the main clause does not force he in the reported clause to refer to the editor.
rationales.The edit merely corrects a plural pronou: They is available for singular personal reference, so the proposed correction is not required by number.

findings: The original agency-at-library item tested elementary its forms under a C1 label.
audit.microSkill: Gender substitution failing to resolve personal ambiguity
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates gender specification from identifying which person a pronoun refers to.
audit.levelReason: An editorial assessment must track two plausible references and avoid supplying information absent from the source.
audit.similarityNote: Evaluates a failed clarification, rather than merely recognizing his ambiguity at B2.

items.setupText: Choose the justified response to the proposed inference.
items.taskText: Report: 'The analyst checked the figures for herself.' Summary: 'The analyst received no assistance while checking the figures.'
options: For herself proves that nobody else had access to the figures.
For herself identifies another analyst as the person who benefited.
For herself means that the analyst checked only figures about her own finances.
For herself can emphasize personal verification without ruling out assistance.
items.answer: For herself can emphasize personal verification without ruling out assistance.
items.explanation: Checking for herself can mean making her own verification. It does not necessarily mean that nobody explained, supplied or helped check the material.

rationales.For herself proves that nobody else had: Personal verification does not establish exclusive access to the material.
rationales.For herself identifies another analyst a: Herself refers back to the analyst, not to a different beneficiary.
rationales.For herself can emphasize personal verif: Checking for herself can mean making her own verification. It does not necessarily mean that nobody explained, supplied or helped check the material.
rationales.For herself means that the analyst check: The reflexive does not identify the figures' subject matter as her personal finances.

findings: The original each-researcher item assumed a feminine reference and rejected her despite a possible other-person beneficiary reading.
audit.microSkill: Personal verification versus an inference of no assistance
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes for oneself from an automatic claim of working entirely unaided.
audit.levelReason: The learner evaluates a subtle strengthening introduced by paraphrasing a reflexive expression.
audit.similarityNote: Limits of for herself, contrasting with explicitly unaided by herself at A2.

items.setupText: Follow the formal editing convention that uses 'who' for subjects and 'whom' for objects. Choose the pair for the two relative clauses.
items.taskText: We appointed the adviser ___ we believed would help us and ___ the team had recommended.
options: whom / who
who / whom
who / who
whom / whom
items.answer: who / whom
items.explanation: 'Who' supplies the subject of 'would help'; 'whom' is the person the team recommended. The intervening reporting words do not determine the first pronoun's case.

rationales.whom / who: The first pronoun is the subject of 'would help' despite intervening 'we believed'; the second is the object of 'had recommended'.
rationales.who / who: The first 'who' fits its subject role. Under the specified formal convention, the object of 'recommended' is 'whom'.
rationales.whom / whom: The second 'whom' fits its object role, but the first pronoun is the subject of 'would help', not the object of 'believed'.
rationales.who / whom: 'Who' supplies the subject of 'would help'; 'whom' is the person the team recommended. The intervening reporting words do not determine the first pronoun's case.

findings: The original proposal-which item offered basic relative-word choices with a stakeholder-meeting tail.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Finds the pronoun's actual clause role instead of choosing case from the nearest verb.
audit.levelReason: Two coordinated relatives require distinguishing embedded subject and object roles under an explicit formal convention.
audit.similarityNote: Embedded role contrast, beyond B2 whom immediately after a preposition.

items.setupText: Choose the criticism of the edit that is supported by the original's institutional reference.
items.taskText: Original: 'The committee adopted the proposal and published its decision.' Edit: 'Every committee member adopted the proposal and published their decision.'
options: The edit changes a unanimous decision into one made by a majority.
The edit only modernizes its to their without changing the actor.
The edit means that several separate committees published one shared decision.
The edit replaces an institutional action with separate actions attributed to every member.
items.answer: The edit replaces an institutional action with separate actions attributed to every member.
items.explanation: The committee and its decision present action at group level. That does not establish each member's individual adoption or publication.

rationales.The edit replaces an institutional actio: The committee and its decision present action at group level. That does not establish each member's individual adoption or publication.
rationales.The edit changes a unanimous decision in: The original does not state unanimity, and the edit does not describe a majority vote.
rationales.The edit only modernizes its to their wi: The subject changes from the committee to every member, so the edit alters more than pronoun style.
rationales.The edit means that several separate com: The edit refers to members of the committee, not to additional committees.

findings: The original keyed the awkward among itself and rejected member-focused themselves without a variety restriction.
audit.microSkill: Institutional possessive reference versus member-by-member attribution
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents a pronoun edit from silently changing the level at which actions are reported.
audit.levelReason: The learner must assess the combined effect of changing both the collective subject and its possessive continuation.
audit.similarityNote: Agency change in a rewrite, not the B2 acceptability of British collective agreement.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation that respects the difference between mutual contradiction and self-contradiction.
items.taskText: The two accounts contradict each other, although neither account contradicts itself.
options: Both accounts contain internal contradictions, but they agree with one another.
One account is internally consistent and the other is not.
Their internal consistency establishes that both give the same true account.
They conflict with one another, but each is internally consistent.
items.answer: They conflict with one another, but each is internally consistent.
items.explanation: Each other links the two accounts in a mutual conflict; itself checks each account against its own contents.

rationales.Both accounts contain internal contradic: This reverses the contrast between each other and itself.
rationales.They conflict with one another, but each: Each other links the two accounts in a mutual conflict; itself checks each account against its own contents.
rationales.One account is internally consistent and: Neither contradicts itself rules out self-contradiction in both accounts, not just one.
rationales.Their internal consistency establishes t: Internal consistency does not erase the stated conflict between the accounts or establish truth.

audit.microSkill: Reciprocal contradiction versus reflexive internal contradiction
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates relations between two texts from consistency within each text.
audit.levelReason: The learner integrates reciprocal and reflexive references with concessive contrast without inferring truth from consistency.
audit.similarityNote: Relational versus internal consistency, not a numerical both/neither paraphrase.

items.setupText: Preserve the source's uncertainty about who was tired; do not guess a referent merely to make the summary shorter.
items.taskText: Source: 'Ari spoke to Morgan because they were tired.' Both people use they/them. The writer confirms that 'they' refers to one person but cannot identify which. Which summary preserves that uncertainty?
options: Ari was tired and therefore spoke to Morgan.
Ari spoke to Morgan because one of them was tired; the source does not identify which person.
Ari spoke to Morgan because Morgan was tired.
Ari and Morgan were both tired when they spoke.
items.answer: Ari spoke to Morgan because one of them was tired; the source does not identify which person.
items.explanation: The summary preserves the confirmed singular reference while leaving its unresolved personal identity open.

rationales.Ari was tired and therefore spoke to Mor: This chooses Ari as the tired person, which the source does not establish.
rationales.Ari spoke to Morgan because Morgan was t: This chooses Morgan as the tired person without source support.
rationales.Ari spoke to Morgan because one of them: The summary preserves the confirmed singular reference while leaving its unresolved personal identity open.
rationales.Ari and Morgan were both tired when they: This chooses a plural reference, contrary to the writer's confirmation that 'they' refers to one person.

findings: The agency-at-museum item repeated elementary possessive spelling instead of testing C1 reference control.
audit.microSkill: Preserving unresolved personal reference in a summary
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids replacing an ambiguous pronoun with a guessed name and presenting the guess as source information.
audit.levelReason: The editing goal is fidelity to uncertainty, not merely making a sentence superficially definite.
audit.similarityNote: Preserves ambiguity deliberately, unlike the B2 brief that supplies the intended office owner.

items.setupText: Choose the report that preserves whose home and whose visit are meant when the listener reports the exchange.
items.taskText: Marta said to Nina, 'Your visit to my home helped me.' Nina later reports Marta's words.
options: Marta said that her visit to my home had helped me.
Marta said that my visit to my home had helped her.
Marta said that my visit to her home had helped her.
Marta said that her visit to her home had helped me.
items.answer: Marta said that my visit to her home had helped her.
items.explanation: Nina reports her own visit as my, while both Marta's home and Marta as beneficiary require her.

rationales.Marta said that her visit to my home had: This reverses the visitor, home owner and beneficiary.
rationales.Marta said that my visit to my home had: Nina's visit was to Marta's home; reporting as Nina does not make the home Nina's.

rationales.Marta said that my visit to her home had: Nina reports her own visit as my, while both Marta's home and Marta as beneficiary require her.

audit.microSkill: Three participant roles remapped by an original listener
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves visitor, possessor and beneficiary through a shift from quotation to report.
audit.levelReason: Several identical third-person forms encode distinct but linked roles, requiring careful perspective tracking.
audit.similarityNote: Listener-as-reporter with a beneficiary, extending the B2 sender/draft/editor mapping.

items.setupText: Choose the accurate response to the editor's objection in standard English.
items.taskText: Draft: 'The proposal, whose cost remains uncertain, has been postponed.' An editor says 'whose' cannot refer to an inanimate proposal.
options: Whose identifies the proposal's author as the person with uncertain costs.
The sentence requires which cost because ownership words only apply to people.
The relative clause explicitly states that cost uncertainty caused the postponement.
Whose can express this relation with an inanimate noun; the proposal's cost is meant.
items.answer: Whose can express this relation with an inanimate noun; the proposal's cost is meant.
items.explanation: 'Whose' is not restricted to human owners. It can link a thing with an associated feature, as with a proposal and its cost.

rationales.Whose can express this relation with an: 'Whose' is not restricted to human owners. It can link a thing with an associated feature, as with a proposal and its cost.
rationales.Whose identifies the proposal's author a: The noun linked to 'cost' is 'proposal'; no author is identified by 'whose'.
rationales.The sentence requires which cost because: 'Which cost' would not supply this possessive relative construction, and the proposed human-only rule is false.
rationales.The relative clause explicitly states th: The clause supplies information about cost, but it does not explicitly assert a causal connection with postponement.

findings: The proposal-which sentence repeated a basic relative choice and changed only the pilot-program tail.
audit.microSkill: Inanimate whose expressing an associated attribute
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids a false human-only restriction while identifying the correct noun-to-attribute relationship.
audit.levelReason: The learner evaluates an editorial rule and interprets a possessive relative in formal prose.
audit.similarityNote: Inanimate attribution, distinct from the B1 employee whose pass identifies a human owner.

items.setupText: Choose the accurate distinction between the possible continuations, without treating either pronoun as automatically ungrammatical.
items.taskText: A series of interviews was recorded. Continuation A: 'It will be released in June.' Continuation B: 'They will be released in June.'
options: A is impossible because the nearest noun interviews is plural.
A refers to the series as a whole; B can refer to the individual interviews.
B proves that the interviews belong to several different series.
A and B both explicitly promise separate release dates for each interview.
items.answer: A refers to the series as a whole; B can refer to the individual interviews.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces both a series and its interviews. The pronoun can select the collective sequence or its individual components.

rationales.A is impossible because the nearest noun: It can refer to the singular head series; proximity to interviews does not block that reference.
rationales.A refers to the series as a whole; B can: The first sentence introduces both a series and its interviews. The pronoun can select the collective sequence or its individual components.
rationales.B proves that the interviews belong to s: Plural reference to interviews does not establish a count of series.
rationales.A and B both explicitly promise separate: Neither version supplies separate dates, and A views the series as a whole.

findings: The original ethics-committee item keyed among itself while excluding a legitimate member-focused themselves reading.
audit.microSkill: Selecting a singular head or plural members as the discourse reference
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes reference choice from mechanical agreement with the nearest visible noun.
audit.levelReason: A complex noun phrase supplies two legitimate discourse entities that different pronouns can select.
audit.similarityNote: Series and component interviews, not a dialect judgment about committee agreement.

items.setupText: Choose the summary that preserves what was marked for review and the reason given, without inventing a conflict between the copies.
items.taskText: The archivist compared two photocopies with the signed original. Neither matched it exactly, so she marked them for review.
options: The archivist flagged the original because both photocopies agreed with one another.
The archivist flagged only one photocopy because the other matched the original.
The archivist flagged both photocopies because each differed from the signed original.
The archivist flagged both photocopies because they contradicted each other.
items.answer: The archivist flagged both photocopies because each differed from the signed original.
items.explanation: Neither applies to the two photocopies, it identifies the original used for comparison, and them returns to the copies marked for review.

rationales.The archivist flagged the original becau: Them refers to the photocopies, not the original, and their agreement with each other is not stated.
rationales.The archivist flagged only one photocopy: Neither matched rejects an exact match for both copies; it does not clear one of them.
rationales.The archivist flagged both photocopies b: Both could differ from the original in the same way. The reason given is failure to match the original, not mutual contradiction.
Neither applies to the two photocopies, it identifies the original used for comparison, and them returns to the copies marked for review.

findings: The original grant-application item keyed the malformed neither can both be correct sequence.
An initial reference-label replacement relied on implausible person/signature distractors; the revised summaries now compete over document roles and comparison relations.
audit.microSkill: Summarizing a reference chain without inventing mutual disagreement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps the checked objects, comparison standard and review targets distinct without adding a relation between the checked objects.
audit.levelReason: The summary must reconstruct three pronoun roles and preserve which comparison supplied the reason for review.
audit.similarityNote: A shared comparison standard does not establish conflict between copies; this is document-reference fidelity, not numerical calculation.

items.setupText: Choose the accurate account of 'it' and the emphasized information.
items.taskText: It was only after the rehearsal that the director changed the ending.
options: It organizes emphasis on the timing; it does not name the rehearsal or the director.
It refers to the ending, which changed the director's decision.
It identifies the director as the only person present at the rehearsal.
It refers to the rehearsal and says that no ending existed before it.
items.answer: It organizes emphasis on the timing; it does not name the rehearsal or the director.
items.explanation: This it-cleft highlights 'only after the rehearsal'. 'It' is a grammatical subject in the emphasis pattern, not a noun reference.

rationales.It refers to the ending, which changed t: The director changes the ending; 'it' does not make the ending an actor.
rationales.It organizes emphasis on the timing; it: This it-cleft highlights 'only after the rehearsal'. 'It' is a grammatical subject in the emphasis pattern, not a noun reference.
rationales.It identifies the director as the only p: 'Only' restricts the timing phrase, not the number of people attending.
rationales.It refers to the rehearsal and says that: The sentence dates a change to the ending; 'it' does not claim that the ending previously did not exist.

findings: The agency-at-airport item repeated elementary possessive spelling with an added legal-review setting.
audit.microSkill: Nonreferential it in a timing-focused cleft
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates grammatical emphasis from noun reference and locates the restriction introduced by only.
audit.levelReason: The reader interprets a cleft construction and its focus without assigning its initial pronoun an invented antecedent.
audit.similarityNote: Cleft emphasis, unlike anticipatory it before an evaluated action.

items.setupText: Choose the ordinary same-clause reference contrast, with no special quotation or perspective-taking context.
items.taskText: A: 'Lena said that Nora had criticized herself.' B: 'Lena said that Nora had criticized her.'
options: In A Nora criticized Nora; B can instead report Nora criticizing Lena or another woman.
Both versions require Nora to have criticized Lena because Lena reports the event.
A makes Lena the critic, whereas B makes Nora the critic.
A and B both establish that Nora criticized an unnamed third woman.
items.answer: In A Nora criticized Nora; B can instead report Nora criticizing Lena or another woman.
items.explanation: Herself links to the local subject Nora. Ordinary her can point outside that local subject relation, including to Lena in the reporting clause.

rationales.Both versions require Nora to have criti: Reporting the event does not make Lena the local reference of herself; the reflexive relates to Nora's action.
rationales.A makes Lena the critic, whereas B makes: Nora is the subject of had criticized in both versions; the object reference is what changes.
rationales.In A Nora criticized Nora; B can instead: Herself links to the local subject Nora. Ordinary her can point outside that local subject relation, including to Lena in the reporting clause.
rationales.A and B both establish that Nora critici: A is self-directed, while B allows but does not require an unnamed third woman.

findings: The original researcher-for-herself risk-assessment item repeated an under-specified reference choice.
audit.microSkill: Local reflexive versus external personal reference in reported content
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes the report's speaker from the actor inside the reported clause.
audit.levelReason: Nested finite clauses supply competing people, and the learner must separate local self-reference from an external reference.
audit.similarityNote: Finite reported-clause contrast, beyond the B1 asked-Ahmed-to infinitive.

items.setupText: Choose the edit that proposes a purchase without presupposing an existing office printer.
items.taskText: Draft: 'Our office has no printer. We should replace it with a more efficient model.' No printer elsewhere has been mentioned.
options: Our office has no printer. We should replace the printer with a more efficient model.
Our office has no printer. It should be repaired before we buy another.
Our office has no printer. We should buy an efficient model.
Our office has no printer. We should replace them with efficient models.
items.answer: Our office has no printer. We should buy an efficient model.
items.explanation: Buy introduces a proposed acquisition without using it to refer to a printer that the preceding sentence says the office lacks.
