rationales.Our office has no printer. It should be: It and repaired still presuppose an existing printer, contrary to the stated context.
rationales.Our office has no printer. We should rep: Pluralizing the pronoun invents multiple existing printers instead of removing the existence assumption.
rationales.Our office has no printer. We should buy: Buy introduces a proposed acquisition without using it to refer to a printer that the preceding sentence says the office lacks.

findings: The original proposal-relative item combined a past revision with after the interviews are coded and retained a basic word choice.
audit.microSkill: Removing a pronoun's unsupported existing-object reference
audit.pedagogicalValue: Repairs reference by changing the action that presupposes an object, not merely repeating or pluralizing its noun.
audit.levelReason: The learner must reconcile discourse existence with the assumptions carried by replace and repair.
audit.similarityNote: Absent-object reference, contrasting with an explicitly planned object's legitimate it in 2735.

items.setupText: Choose what role 'as such' resumes in this sentence.
items.taskText: Jules attends the board meetings as an observer, not as a voting member; as such, Jules may comment but may not vote.
options: Jules's role as a voting member.
The board's right to vote on Jules's comments.
Jules's role as an observer.
The fact that Jules has already voted at several meetings.
items.answer: Jules's role as an observer.
items.explanation: 'As such' resumes the affirmed observer role. The denied voting-member role does not become its reference just because it is nearer.

'As such' resumes the affirmed observer role. The denied voting-member role does not become its reference just because it is nearer.
'Not as a voting member' explicitly denies that role; the nearest role phrase is not automatically the reference.
rationales.The board's right to vote on Jules's com: 'As such' links Jules's status to Jules's permissions, not the board's response to comments.
rationales.The fact that Jules has already voted at: Attendance is stated, but voting is expressly prohibited and no earlier votes are reported.

findings: The assessment-committee tasks item keyed among itself and rejected collective alternatives without a stated variety.
audit.microSkill: As such resuming an affirmed rather than a negated role
audit.pedagogicalValue: Tracks a role-based reference through an intervening explicitly rejected description.
audit.levelReason: The learner must integrate discourse contrast and status-based reference rather than select the nearest noun phrase.
audit.similarityNote: Role reference with as such, not a personal subject/object pronoun.

items.setupText: Choose the accurate assessment of 'it' in this project note.
items.taskText: We are designing a portable scanner. It must fit inside a coat pocket, although no prototype exists yet.
options: It proves that at least one complete scanner is already available.
It can refer to the planned scanner without implying that it already exists as a built object.
It must refer to the coat pocket because only existing objects can be pronoun references.
It refers to the design team collectively rather than to the scanner.
items.answer: It can refer to the planned scanner without implying that it already exists as a built object.
items.explanation: Discourse can introduce a planned or imagined object and continue referring to that object with a pronoun.

rationales.It proves that at least one complete sca: The scanner is introduced as a design target, and the note explicitly says no prototype exists.
rationales.It can refer to the planned scanner with: Discourse can introduce a planned or imagined object and continue referring to that object with a pronoun.
rationales.It must refer to the coat pocket because: The pocket is a later size constraint; the pronoun refers to the planned scanner, and physical existence is not required.
rationales.It refers to the design team collectivel: The size requirement concerns the scanner, not the people designing it.

findings: The appendix-note variant preserved the malformed neither can both be correct sequence.
audit.microSkill: Pronoun reference to a planned object
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids imposing a physical-existence requirement on every pronoun reference.
audit.levelReason: The learner reconciles ongoing design, a pronoun-based requirement and explicit nonexistence of a prototype.
audit.similarityNote: Legitimate conceptual reference contrasts with the unsupported replace-it presupposition in 2733.

items.setupText: Choose the edit that makes the draft, rather than either writer, the explicit object needing further work.
items.taskText: Note: 'The editor compared Mara's draft with Ivo's response. She thought the former needed further work.' The editor confirms that she meant Mara's draft.
options: The editor thought Mara's draft needed further work.
The editor thought Mara needed further work on Ivo's response.
The editor thought Ivo's response needed further work.
The editor thought the former writer needed further work.
items.answer: The editor thought Mara's draft needed further work.
items.explanation: The explicit noun phrase preserves the intended document reference without relying on a formal backward-pointing label.

rationales.The editor thought Mara needed further w: This makes Mara the person who needs to work on the response instead of identifying her draft as the object needing revision.
rationales.The editor thought Ivo's response needed: This identifies the second text rather than the confirmed draft.
rationales.The editor thought Mara's draft needed f: The explicit noun phrase preserves the intended document reference without relying on a formal backward-pointing label.
rationales.The editor thought the former writer nee: Adding writer changes the reference from a text to a person and does not identify the draft.

findings: The agency-at-market item was another elementary its/it's choice with a new location and audit tail.
audit.microSkill: Expanding a formal reference without changing text into author
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps a possessive document phrase intact when replacing former with an explicit name.
audit.levelReason: An editorial expansion must preserve the head noun draft rather than selecting its embedded owner's name.
audit.similarityNote: Referent expansion from a possessive text phrase, not simply ordering former and latter.

items.setupText: Choose what the phrase 'This limitation' refers to and adds to the discussion.
items.taskText: The survey excluded people who worked night shifts. This limitation makes its findings less useful for planning overnight services.
options: It identifies the night workers' decision to withdraw as the source of the limitation.
It identifies a restriction imposed by the overnight services on the researchers.
It identifies a coverage gap but says the findings apply only to night workers.
It identifies the exclusion as a limitation relevant to the findings' use.
items.answer: It identifies the exclusion as a limitation relevant to the findings' use.
items.explanation: 'This' points back to the exclusion, while 'limitation' categorizes that event as a constraint on applying the findings.

rationales.It identifies the night workers' decisio: 'Excluded' reports their omission from the survey, not a decision by the workers to withdraw.
rationales.It identifies a restriction imposed by t: The limitation belongs to the survey's coverage; the services are the intended use of its findings.
rationales.It identifies a coverage gap but says th: The gap makes application to night workers less useful, not exclusive or especially well supported.
rationales.It identifies the exclusion as a limitat: 'This' points back to the exclusion, while 'limitation' categorizes that event as a constraint on applying the findings.

findings: The protocol-review researcher item repeated ambiguous for-herself reference with generic messages.
audit.microSkill: An evaluative reference noun summarizing a preceding proposition
audit.pedagogicalValue: Sees that this plus a summary noun both refers backward and categorizes what is referred to.
audit.levelReason: The learner interprets the referential and evaluative work of one cohesive phrase in analytical prose.
audit.similarityNote: Evaluative encapsulation, not bare This replacing a cancellation event.

items.setupText: Choose the expansion that preserves the omitted noun and verb in the second clause.
items.taskText: Some objections concerned cost; others, access to the building.
options: Other objectors were concerned about the building's cost.
Other buildings were accessible only at an additional cost.
Other objections concerned access to the building.
The same objections concerned both cost and access to the building.
items.answer: Other objections concerned access to the building.
items.explanation: Others replaces other objections, and the second clause omits the repeated verb concerned.

rationales.Other objections concerned access to the: Others replaces other objections, and the second clause omits the repeated verb concerned.
rationales.Other objectors were concerned about the: This changes objections into people and repeats cost instead of preserving the access topic.
rationales.Other buildings were accessible only at: Others refers to objections, not buildings, and no additional access charge is stated.
rationales.The same objections concerned both cost: Others introduces different objections, not another topic assigned to the same subset.

findings: The proposal revised on the evidence table retained the basic which gap with an unnatural appended setting.
audit.microSkill: Others and omitted predicate in parallel clauses
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recovers both a noun category and an omitted verb without replacing statements with their speakers.
audit.levelReason: Compressed analytical prose requires reconstruction of two omitted elements and preservation of the contrasted groups.
audit.similarityNote: Pronoun-plus-verb omission, beyond B1 standalone any with one omitted noun.

items.setupText: Choose the accurate reading of the two references to the novel.
items.taskText: The novel itself I enjoyed; its publicity campaign I found exhausting.
options: Itself emphasizes the novel as distinct from the campaign associated with it.
Itself says that the narrator read the novel without assistance.
Its refers to the writer's personal campaign rather than the novel's publicity.
The sentence says the publicity campaign was enjoyable but the novel was exhausting.
items.answer: Itself emphasizes the novel as distinct from the campaign associated with it.
items.explanation: The self form focuses the novel in contrast with its publicity. Its then links the campaign to that novel.

rationales.Itself says that the narrator read the n: The self form emphasizes the novel as an object, not the reader's independence or method of reading.
rationales.Itself emphasizes the novel as distinct: The self form focuses the novel in contrast with its publicity. Its then links the campaign to that novel.
rationales.Its refers to the writer's personal camp: The established reference is the novel; no separate writer's campaign is introduced.
rationales.The sentence says the publicity campaign: This reverses the evaluations assigned to the two fronted objects.

findings: The disciplinary-committee item repeated the awkward among itself key and unexplained rejection of member-focused reference.
audit.microSkill: Emphatic and possessive reference with fronted objects
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps actor, evaluated object and associated possession distinct despite marked word order.
audit.levelReason: Two fronted objects require reading beyond normal subject-first order while interpreting different self and possessive functions.
audit.similarityNote: Object fronting and contrastive emphasis, not the B2 departments/problem minimal pair.

items.setupText: The intended meaning is that my respect for Nora is greater than her manager's respect for Nora. Choose the explicit rewrite.
items.taskText: Draft: 'I respect Nora more than her manager.'
options: I respect Nora more than her manager respects her.
I respect Nora more than I respect her manager.
Nora respects me more than she respects her manager.
Her manager respects Nora more than I respect her.
items.answer: I respect Nora more than her manager respects her.
items.explanation: The repeated verb identifies the manager as the second person doing the respecting; her refers back to Nora as its object.

rationales.I respect Nora more than I respect her m: This compares the speaker's respect for two people, not two people's respect for Nora.
rationales.Nora respects me more than she respects: This makes Nora the person showing respect rather than its recipient.
rationales.I respect Nora more than her manager res: The repeated verb identifies the manager as the second person doing the respecting; her refers back to Nora as its object.
rationales.Her manager respects Nora more than I re: This reverses which person has the greater respect for Nora.

findings: The final assessment-rubric item retained the ungrammatical keyed neither can both be correct sentence.
audit.microSkill: Resolving a comparative clause's omitted actor and object
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses an explicit verb and pronoun to distinguish two possible comparisons hidden by omission.
audit.levelReason: A fluent comparative ambiguity must be expanded while preserving both participant roles and comparison direction.
audit.similarityNote: Comparative clause recovery, distinct from noun-only that of substitution.

items.setupText: Choose the criticism that identifies the unsupported implication introduced by the rewrite.
items.taskText: Original: 'The committee members disagreed among themselves in front of the reporters.' Rewrite: 'The committee members kept their disagreement to themselves.'
options: The rewrite turns disagreement within the group into concealment from outsiders.
The rewrite merely changes a group discussion into several individual disagreements.
The rewrite preserves public disagreement but says that the members resolved it privately.
The rewrite changes disagreement within the committee into disagreement with the reporters.
items.answer: The rewrite turns disagreement within the group into concealment from outsiders.
items.explanation: Among themselves locates the disagreement between members; keep something to oneself concerns not sharing it. The reporters' presence makes that change consequential.

rationales.The rewrite merely changes a group discu: Kept their disagreement to themselves introduces nondisclosure, not simply a different distribution of disagreements.
rationales.The rewrite turns disagreement within th: Among themselves locates the disagreement between members; keep something to oneself concerns not sharing it. The reporters' presence makes that change consequential.
rationales.The rewrite preserves public disagreemen: Kept to themselves does not report a resolution, and it changes the public-disclosure implication.
rationales.The rewrite changes disagreement within: The reflexive phrase does not make reporters the opposing party; it concerns whether the members disclosed their disagreement.

findings: The original committee-members item labeled a basic reflexive-form gap C2 and supplied generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Among themselves versus keeping something to themselves
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes internal participant reference from an idiomatic claim of nondisclosure.
audit.levelReason: An apparently economical rewrite changes the function of a reflexive expression and the public status of an event.
audit.similarityNote: Disclosure implications of reflexive idioms, not who performed a task unaided.

items.setupText: Use the formal convention that selects 'whoever' for a subject within its clause and 'whomever' for an object within its clause.
items.taskText: The task will go to ___ the panel believes can finish it; the panel will consult ___ the chair recommends.
options: whomever / whoever
whoever / whoever
whoever / whomever
whomever / whomever
items.answer: whoever / whomever
items.explanation: The whole first clause follows 'to', but 'whoever' is the subject inside that clause. 'Whomever' is the person the chair recommends in the second clause.

rationales.whomever / whoever: In the first clause, the pronoun is the subject of 'can finish' despite the preceding 'to'. In the second it is the object of 'recommends'.
rationales.whoever / whoever: The first form matches its subject role; the second requires the object form under the stated formal convention.
rationales.whoever / whomever: The whole first clause follows 'to', but 'whoever' is the subject inside that clause. 'Whomever' is the person the chair recommends in the second clause.
rationales.whomever / whomever: The second form fits. The first incorrectly chooses case from the outer preposition rather than the pronoun's role as subject of 'can finish'.

findings: The original question-of-who item repeated one case distinction with unrelated specialist tails and no diagnostic explanation.
audit.microSkill: Case inside free-relative clauses despite outer object positions
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates the role of an entire clause from the grammatical role of the pronoun within it.
audit.levelReason: Two free relatives interact with an intervening reporting clause and an outer preposition under an explicit formal style convention.
audit.similarityNote: Free-relative case at two structural levels, extending rather than repeating the C1 headed-relative contrast.

items.setupText: Choose the summary that preserves both the source of the criticism and the self-directed relation it alleges.
items.taskText: The dissent accuses the majority of contradicting itself; the editor has not assessed whether that accusation is justified.
options: According to the dissent, the majority's position conflicts with its own position elsewhere.
The majority says that the dissent contradicts the majority's position.
The editor confirms that the majority's position is internally contradictory.
The dissent claims that the majority disagrees with the dissent.
items.answer: According to the dissent, the majority's position conflicts with its own position elsewhere.
items.explanation: According to preserves attribution to the dissent, while its own retains the self-contradiction alleged of the majority.

rationales.The majority says that the dissent contr: This reverses the source and target and replaces alleged self-contradiction with disagreement between two parties.
rationales.The editor confirms that the majority's: The editor has not assessed the accusation, so confirmation removes the stated attribution limit.
rationales.The dissent claims that the majority dis: That is disagreement with another party; itself alleges a conflict within the majority's own position.
rationales.According to the dissent, the majority's: According to preserves attribution to the dissent, while its own retains the self-contradiction alleged of the majority.

findings: The original majority-itself gap excluded legitimate collective readings without a variety or meaning criterion.
audit.microSkill: Attributed self-contradiction without endorsing or redirecting it
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps the critic, criticized party and internal reference distinct when summarizing an allegation.
audit.levelReason: A faithful paraphrase must simultaneously preserve attribution and a reflexive relation rather than substitute mutual disagreement.
audit.similarityNote: Source-sensitive reflexive reporting, unlike C1's direct comparison of mutual and internal contradiction.

items.setupText: Choose the revision that preserves reliance on the estimate without expanding it into general reliance on its author.
items.taskText: The expert on whose estimate the panel relied later withdrew that estimate.
options: The panel relied on the expert's estimate, which the expert later withdrew.
The panel relied on the expert, who later withdrew from the panel.
The expert relied on the panel's estimate and later withdrew it.
The panel relied on the expert's later withdrawal of the estimate.
items.answer: The panel relied on the expert's estimate, which the expert later withdrew.
items.explanation: Whose connects the estimate to the expert, while on makes the estimate the object of reliance. The rewrite retains both relationships.

rationales.The panel relied on the expert's estimat: Whose connects the estimate to the expert, while on makes the estimate the object of reliance. The rewrite retains both relationships.
rationales.The panel relied on the expert, who late: This changes reliance on an estimate into reliance on a person and changes withdrawing an estimate into leaving the panel.
rationales.The expert relied on the panel's estimat: This reverses who relied on whose estimate.
rationales.The panel relied on the expert's later w: The original makes the estimate, not its withdrawal, the basis of the panel's reliance.

findings: The original on-whom expert item repeated a formal object-pronoun gap with a fiduciary-briefing tail.
audit.microSkill: Possessive relative reference inside a fronted prepositional phrase
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes the author, the author's claim and a later action involving that claim.
audit.levelReason: The learner expands an embedded possessive relative while preserving two relations and the later pronoun's object identity.
audit.similarityNote: A person's attributed estimate as the reference unit, not a bare to-whom recipient.

items.setupText: In the first clause, 'her' means "Rosa's". Choose the accurate assessment of the editor's expansion of the omitted verb phrase.
items.taskText: Original: 'Rosa revised her abstract, and Nina did too.' Edit: 'Rosa revised her abstract, and Nina revised Rosa's abstract too.'
options: The edit is required because omitted words must keep every possessive reference unchanged.
The edit contradicts the original, which requires Nina to revise a different abstract.
The edit adds that Rosa revised Nina's abstract before revising her own.
The edit selects a shared-abstract reading; the original also allows Nina to revise her own abstract.
items.answer: The edit selects a shared-abstract reading; the original also allows Nina to revise her own abstract.
items.explanation: 'Did too' can mean "revised Rosa's abstract" or 'revised her own abstract' with Nina as the new subject. Naming Rosa removes the second reading.

rationales.The edit is required because omitted wor: Ellipsis can preserve Rosa's abstract or adapt the possessive relation so that Nina revises Nina's own abstract.
rationales.The edit selects a shared-abstract readi: 'Did too' can mean "revised Rosa's abstract" or 'revised her own abstract' with Nina as the new subject. Naming Rosa removes the second reading.
rationales.The edit contradicts the original, which: The original permits the shared-abstract reading; it does not require a different abstract for Nina.
rationales.The edit adds that Rosa revised Nina's a: The first clause still refers only to Rosa revising Rosa's abstract; the edit clarifies the object of Nina's action.

findings: The original each-objection-its gap was an elementary possessive-form choice disguised by a methodological tail.
audit.microSkill: Possessive reference under verb-phrase ellipsis
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes that restoring omitted wording can select between a fixed owner's object and the new subject's own object.
audit.levelReason: The learner must distinguish two licensed readings of an elliptical clause and evaluate an edit that resolves them.
audit.similarityNote: Fixed versus subject-relative ownership under ellipsis, not the determiners topic's shared existential witness.

items.setupText: Choose the report that preserves the memoirist's move from personal experience to a general reflection, without turning it into an accusation against the interviewer.
items.taskText: Asked about leaving her hometown, the memoirist says, 'At first I missed it terribly. You don't realize what a place means to you until you leave.'
options: She describes her own loss, then frames a general reflection about leaving a familiar place.
She says the interviewer failed to appreciate the hometown before leaving it.
She changes her account by saying that she never missed the hometown herself.
She reports that every person who leaves any place has exactly her experience.
items.answer: She describes her own loss, then frames a general reflection about leaving a familiar place.
items.explanation: The shift from I to generic you broadens the reflection and invites identification without assigning the experience to the specific listener.

rationales.She says the interviewer failed to appre: Generic you need not identify the interviewer as someone who lived there or failed to appreciate it.
rationales.She changes her account by saying that s: The general you statement does not retract the preceding first-person report.
rationales.She describes her own loss, then frames: The shift from I to generic you broadens the reflection and invites identification without assigning the experience to the specific listener.
rationales.She reports that every person who leaves: A reflective generic you does not establish that universal, identical experience for every person and place.

findings: The hiring-committee chart item repeated a basic themselves gap under a C2 label.
audit.microSkill: Personal narrative broadening through generic you
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves a rhetorical shift without converting it into a direct personal charge or an exceptionless factual generalization.
audit.levelReason: The reader interprets changing participant perspective and the force of a generalizing voice within quoted reflective discourse.
audit.similarityNote: Autobiographical generalization, distinct from generic you in practical travel instructions.

items.setupText: Choose the report that preserves the quoted speaker's group without adding the journalist to it.
items.taskText: Speaking for the restoration team, the curator told a journalist, 'We repaired the frame ourselves, but our conservator restored the paint.' The journalist was not part of the team.
options: The curator and journalist repaired the frame; their conservator restored the paint.
The team repaired the frame itself; its conservator restored the paint.
The conservator repaired the frame alone and the team restored the paint.
The journalist joined the team in repairing both the frame and the paint.
items.answer: The team repaired the frame itself; its conservator restored the paint.
items.explanation: The quoted we and ourselves refer to the restoration team. Its conservator preserves the team relationship while keeping the two tasks distinct.

rationales.The curator and journalist repaired the: The quote's we belongs to the restoration team, not to the speaker and every person listening.
rationales.The conservator repaired the frame alone: This reverses the allocation of work between the team and its conservator.
rationales.The journalist joined the team in repair: The context excludes the journalist from the team, and the paint restoration is assigned to the conservator.
rationales.The team repaired the frame itself; its: The quoted we and ourselves refer to the restoration team. Its conservator preserves the team relationship while keeping the two tasks distinct.

findings: The statute question-of-who sentence recycled one case distinction with an interpretive-framework tail.
audit.microSkill: Exclusive quoted we and reflexive agency in external reporting
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps a quoted institutional group separate from the addressee and preserves the allocation of its work.
audit.levelReason: The report must map three first-person group references to an external perspective without merging task performers.
audit.similarityNote: Exclusive quoted group with divided tasks, not B2 reader-inclusive we.

items.setupText: Choose who the two first-person forms refer to at their different quotation levels.
items.taskText: In her diary, Leila writes: 'When my brother arrived, I told him, "You can stay in my room."' A biographer quotes this entry without changing it.
options: I refers to the biographer, while my in the offer refers to Leila.
I refers to Leila, but my in the offer refers to her brother because he is the listener.
I in the narration and my in the offer both refer to Leila.
Both forms refer to the brother because the entry begins with his arrival.
items.answer: I in the narration and my in the offer both refer to Leila.
items.explanation: Leila is the diary's first-person narrator and the speaker of the nested offer. Quoting the entry does not transfer those first-person references to the biographer.

rationales.I in the narration and my in the offer b: Leila is the diary's first-person narrator and the speaker of the nested offer. Quoting the entry does not transfer those first-person references to the biographer.
rationales.I refers to the biographer, while my in: The biographer is quoting Leila's text, not adopting the diary's I as a self-reference.
rationales.I refers to Leila, but my in the offer r: My is determined by the offer's speaker, Leila; you addresses her brother.
rationales.Both forms refer to the brother because: Being the first participant mentioned does not make the brother the speaker of Leila's narration or offer.

findings: The appellate-review majority item repeated an under-specified collective reflexive choice.
audit.microSkill: First-person reference preserved through nested and external quotation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps a quotation's speaker distinct from its addressee and from a later author reproducing it.
audit.levelReason: Three discourse roles and two quotation levels must be tracked without shifting ownership to the nearest voice.
audit.similarityNote: Nested exact quotation, unlike indirect reporting that actively changes pronoun forms.

items.setupText: Choose the edit that preserves the witness as the source of both the discovery claim and the description; the narrator has verified neither.
items.taskText: Draft: 'The witness said that police had found a weapon. It was rusty.' The intended source of 'rusty' is also the witness.
options: Police found a weapon, which the witness said was rusty.
The witness said that police had found a weapon and that it was rusty.
The witness said police had found a weapon, and the narrator confirmed that it was rusty.
The weapon was rusty, although the witness denied that police had found it.
items.answer: The witness said that police had found a weapon and that it was rusty.
items.explanation: The repeated 'that' explicitly places both linked claims inside the witness's report; 'it' continues the same weapon reference without claiming narrator verification.

rationales.Police found a weapon, which the witness: This places the discovery outside the witness's reported claim and presents it as the narrator's assertion.
rationales.The witness said that police had found a: The repeated 'that' explicitly places both linked claims inside the witness's report; 'it' continues the same weapon reference without claiming narrator verification.
rationales.The witness said police had found a weap: The narrator has confirmed neither claim; this adds independent verification of the condition.
rationales.The weapon was rusty, although the witne: This asserts the condition directly and turns the witness's discovery claim into a denial.

findings: The technical-memorandum on-whom item repeated a formal pronoun case choice with basic competing forms.
audit.microSkill: Keeping a continued object reference inside its reported source
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids letting a short it sentence appear to promote reported information into the narrator's own verified account.
audit.levelReason: A cohesive rewrite must preserve object identity and the attribution scope of two linked propositions.
audit.similarityNote: Reported object's descriptive continuation, not merely identifying an accusation's critic.

items.setupText: Choose the paraphrase that retains the objection as the source of the standards used to assess it, without claiming agreement with it.
items.taskText: The reply examines the objection on its own terms before challenging its assumptions.
options: The reply evaluates the objection solely by the reply's own preferred standards.
The reply accepts the objection's assumptions and therefore abandons its challenge.
The reply challenges only the objection's wording while accepting its assumptions.
The reply first assesses the objection within its stated framework, then questions that framework's assumptions.
items.answer: The reply first assesses the objection within its stated framework, then questions that framework's assumptions.
items.explanation: Both possessives maintain the objection as the reference. Taking its framework seriously for assessment is compatible with subsequently challenging its assumptions.

rationales.The reply evaluates the objection solely: Its own terms points to the objection's framework, not simply the reply's preferred standards.
rationales.The reply accepts the objection's assump: Examining an objection on its own terms does not entail accepting it, and the later challenge is explicitly retained.
rationales.The reply first assesses the objection w: Both possessives maintain the objection as the reference. Taking its framework seriously for assessment is compatible with subsequently challenging its assumptions.
rationales.The reply challenges only the objection': The stated later target is its assumptions, not merely the words used to express them.

findings: The original framework/objection sentence repeated an elementary its/it's gap beneath an objections-synthesized tail.
audit.microSkill: Perspective-sensitive its own terms without implied endorsement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps the source of evaluative standards distinct from the evaluator's acceptance of those standards.
audit.levelReason: Two possessive references and a staged argumentative relation must be preserved without turning provisional perspective-taking into agreement.
audit.similarityNote: Argumentative perspective and ownership of standards, not a physical object's owner.

items.setupText: Choose the accurate assessment of the demonstrative reference, not merely of the repeated wording.
items.taskText: Standing at the north entrance, Bea says, 'This door was locked.' Later, standing at the south entrance, Tom says the same words. An editor writes, 'They identified the same locked door.'
options: The shared wording requires Tom's this to refer back to Bea's north entrance.
The editor is wrong because the speakers necessarily disagree about which doors were locked.
The repeated this establishes that Tom is quoting Bea instead of making his own observation.
Identical words do not establish identical reference when this is used from different positions.
items.answer: Identical words do not establish identical reference when this is used from different positions.
items.explanation: This is interpreted from the speaker's situation. The two speakers can use the same sentence while pointing to different doors, so the editor's shared-door claim is unsupported.

rationales.Identical words do not establish identic: This is interpreted from the speaker's situation. The two speakers can use the same sentence while pointing to different doors, so the editor's shared-door claim is unsupported.
rationales.The shared wording requires Tom's this t: Tom's demonstrative can be anchored in his own location; it need not inherit Bea's reference.
rationales.The editor is wrong because the speakers: They may describe different locked doors without disagreeing; different reference is not contradiction.
rationales.The repeated this establishes that Tom i: Using the same demonstrative wording does not establish quotation; the stated scene presents Tom speaking from his own position.

findings: The language-committee lesson-plan item repeated the elementary among-themselves frame.
audit.microSkill: Context-dependent demonstrative reference despite identical wording
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes matching sentences from reference to the same real-world object.
audit.levelReason: An editorial inference must account for two speech contexts and avoid equating verbal identity with referential identity.
audit.similarityNote: Deictic context across repeated quotations, not a quantified shared-witness inference.

items.setupText: The writer means that adopting the fallback plan would have been disastrous. Choose the continuation that states that unrealized action explicitly.
items.taskText: Opening: 'Dana rejected our only fallback plan.' Draft continuation: 'It would have been a disaster.'
options: Dana's rejection of the fallback plan was a disaster.
Rejecting that fallback plan would have been a disaster.
The absence of any fallback plan had already caused a disaster.
Adopting that fallback plan would have been a disaster.
items.answer: Adopting that fallback plan would have been a disaster.
items.explanation: The explicit action phrase supplies the intended reference for it and preserves the unrealized adoption being evaluated.

rationales.Dana's rejection of the fallback plan wa: This evaluates the actual rejection instead of the unrealized adoption, and changes the counterfactual wording to an actual verdict.
rationales.Adopting that fallback plan would have b: The explicit action phrase supplies the intended reference for it and preserves the unrealized adoption being evaluated.
rationales.Rejecting that fallback plan would have: This preserves the hypothetical form but assigns the negative evaluation to rejection, the opposite intended action.

findings: The statute-with-corrigendum item repeated a who/whom gap without a new advanced reference task.
